### Ontology analyses using diffused networks

#### Data generation

The method employed here is similar to the one developed in Giudice et al., 2024. Briefly, we retrieved the Drosophila protein-protein interaction network from IntAct (last update June 2020). We modeled the edge weights (Resnik, 1999) using the Resnik semantic similarity, which was calculated using the Semantic Measures Library (Harispe et al., 2014). We also generated 1000 random networks, where the node degrees are conserved, employing the vl method from the igraph library (Latapy, 2016). The edge weights of the random network are updated accordingly. To correct for the hub bias, we applied the Laplacian normalization to all networks using:

$$
w_{ij}=\frac{w_{ij}}{\sqrt{d_{i}d_{j}}}
$$

where $w_{ij}$ indicates the edge weight and $d_{i}$ and $d_{j}$ represent the weighted degree of node i and node j respectively. We extracted from the Pfam (Mistry et al., 2021) database (last update June 2021), all the kinases detected in Drosophila by selecting the CL0016 clan. Next, we employed the UniprotKB database to distinguish the tyrosine kinases (family: PF07714) from other kinases. In total 56 tyrosine kinases and 251 other kinases are present in the network. We also precalculated the mean and the standard deviation of the Resnik semantic similarity of each regulated node in the network against each other.

### Seed selection and network diffusion

We applied the random-walk-with-restart-based algorithm (Giudice et al., 2024) for the following DV clusters: D (1), L (2), V (5), DL (6), DV (9) and LV (12), once each for the ED score and once for the deviation values, and each for the protein and phosphoproteomic datasets. In the case of the deviation values, we used only those proteins or phosphosites within the interquartile range. We assigned as seed value the reciprocal of the absolute value from both the ED Score or the log2 Fold Change Deviations. Note that if multiple phosphosites are assigned to the same protein we selected the median of the ED scores or log2 Deviations. We then partition the seed set in tyrosine kinases, remaining kinases and other proteins and perform the random walk with restart (RWR) from each of the three partitions separately. We also repeated the same procedure with the same set of initial nodes against 1000 random networks. We estimated the empirical p-value for each node of the network as the percent of its random scores that exceed the real score and selected only the nodes with a p-value <0.05 in at least one of the three partitions. The resulting subnetworks are further filtered using the ego decomposition (Giudice et al., 2024). Briefly, for each seed node we extracted ego networks with a maximum distance of 2 steps from the ego. We then filtered the ego networks by selecting only the most similar functional nodes to the ego using this formula:

$$
z−score=\frac{Resnik(ego,j)−mean_{Resnikego}}{std_{Resnikego}}
$$

where $Resnik(ego,j)$ is the semantic similarity between the ego and a node j in the ego network, $mean_{Resnikego}andstd_{Resnikego}$ are the mean and the standard deviation of the ego against all the other nodes in the initial network. Nodes with a z-score>1.28 (equivalent to a p-value <0.1) are retained. After this filtering, the resulting ego networks with less than 5 nodes are discarded. Additionally, the weight of the ego networks are changed according to (3) to reflect the functional impact of the dysregulation of the ego on the neighboring nodes.

$$
w(i,j)={Resnik(ego,j)ifi=egoandj=Γ_{ego}ori=Γ_{ego}andj=Γ_{Γ_{ego}}\frac{Resnik(ego,i)+Resnik(ego,j)}{2}ifi=Γ_{ego}andj=Γ_{ego}ori=Γ_{Γ_{ego}}andj=Γ_{Γ_{ego}}
$$

where Γ(ego) represents the nodes at distance 1 from the ego and ΓΓ(ego) represents the nodes at distance 2 from the ego. The ego networks obtained are normalized again to correct for hubs using the Laplacian normalization using (1). For each ego network, we then calculate the topological distance vector and the functional distance vector as in Giudice et al. The topological distance vector is calculated using the following formula (4):

$$
topologicaldistance=1000\timeslog_{2}(1−jsd(RWR_{node},RWR_{ego}))
$$

where $jsd$ refers to the Jensen-Shannon distance, representing the similarity between two probability distributions. The RWRnode refers to the RWR probability vector when one of the nodes of the ego network is selected as seed, and the RWRego refers to the RWR probability vector when the ego is the seed node. The functional vector is defined as the logarithm of the semantic similarity between the ego and any other nodes in the network (5).

$$
functionaldistance=1000\timeslog_{2}(Resnik(ego,node))
$$

where Resnik(ego, node) represents the semantic similarity measure between the ego and the node under consideration. To assess the most similar nodes to the ego, the Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) measure (with Gaussian kernel and bandwidth estimated using the Silvermann formula) to assess the most similar nodes to the ego, is employed. KDE estimates the probability density function (PDF) of the topological and semantic similarity vectors obtained at the previous step. For each ego network, we selected only those nodes within a 0.7≤PDF ≤ 1.0 of both topological and functional similarity. All the nodes overcoming this threshold are selected for the enrichment analysis against the cellular component domain of GO.

### Ontology analyses of extreme deviating proteins and phosphoproteins using PANTHER protein class

We filtered the proteins and phosphosites with an absolute log2 deviation value larger than the 95th percentile (prctile Matlab function) of the distribution of absolute log2 deviation values. Because deviation values were calculated separately for each ventralized genotype (Toll10B/df or spn27Aex/df), we obtained two independent lists of proteins and phosphosites with deviation values exceeding the 95th percentile. From these lists, we selected the proteins and phosphosites whose log2 deviations exceeded the 95th percentile threshold with both ventralized genotypes. For phosphosites, we used the host phosphoprotein for the ontology analyses. When two or more phosphosites with large deviations were hosted by the same phosphoprotein, we counted the phosphoprotein only once. We therefore obtained 206 proteins and 154 phosphoproteins (191 phosphosites) that were used in the ontology analyses.

The ontology analyses were performed using the PANTHER platform (http://www.pantherdb.org/, release PANTHER 17.0 dated February 23rd 2022). We queried the 'Functional classification gene list', based on 'Drosophila melanogaster' organism data. We used the FBgn (Flybase Gene Number) of the proteins and phosphoproteins to produce the query in Panther, and focused on the 'Protein Class' classification. The protein class query allocated 125/206 proteins and 110/154 phosphoproteins to protein class terms. Using gene ontologies from Flybase we manually allocated 48/206 proteins and 35/154 phosphoproteins to one or more of the 24 parental protein class categories. 33/206 proteins and 9/154 phosphoproteins could not be allocated to any parental class category, remained unassigned and were therefore excluded from the reported analyses. In summary, the reported protein class ontology analyses of extremely deviating proteins and phosphoproteins is based on 173/206 proteins and 145/154 phosphoproteins.

### Functional perturbations on microtubules

#### Depolymerisation of microtubules and imaging

Embryos laid by flies heterozygous for EMTB-3xGFP and 3xmScarlet-CaaX transgenes or EGFP-CaaX and H2Av-mRFP1 (Schuh et al., 2007) transgenes were submerged under Halocarbon oil 27 (Sigma-Aldrich) for staging. Early cellularizing embryos were selected, dechorionated with 50% bleach after removal of Halocarbon oil, washed with H2O, mounted with heptane glue on a coverslip, desiccated with silica gel or Drierite for 10’–15’, and subsequently covered with a 3:1 mixture of Halocarbon 700 and 27 oils. For Colcemid injection, 4 mg/ml Demecolcine (Sigma-Aldrich) in H2O was injected with a custom-made injection needle that was prepared from a borosilicate glass micropipette (Drummond) with a Sutter Instrument pipette puller (P-97/IVF) and a Narishige grinder (EG-44). The stage of injection was controlled based on the transmission brightfield image. A volume of ~65 pL, measured with a 20 X dry lens via an objective micrometre, was injected into the middle section of embryos. Injection was performed with a Narishige IM400 setup mounted on a Nikon Ti2/Eclipse inverted microscope equipped and under a 60 x/NA1.42 oil immersion objective. Imaging was performed on a Yokogawa CSU-W1/SORA imaging system mounted on the same scope. Two laser lines (488 and 561 nm) were used to excite the sample, while a tandem of sCMOS cameras (Prime BSI, Teledyne Photometrics) were used to acquire the image with 2x2 binning. A single z-stack volume was acquired prior to injection, followed by a post-injection z-stack time series. The gap between pre-injection and post-injection imaging was typically 2’~3’. CSU-SORA 4 x zoom was used for imaging EMTB-3xGFP and 3xmScarlet-CaaX with a z-step size of 0.3 μm and a total z-depth of 6.3 μm at a rate of 30 s per volume, while CSU-W1 was used for EGFP-CaaX and H2Av-mRFP1 with a z-step size of 1 μm and a total z-depth of 40 μm at a rate of 1’ per volume.

### Image processing and quantitation

For quantitation of nuclear position, single z-slice H2Av-mRFP1 images were converted into tiff format, blurred with a Gaussian filter (σ=2), and segmented with CellPose (v2.2) in 2D using a custom-pretrained nuclear model tailored for each side of the embryo based on manual correction on segmentation generated by a default nuclei model with nuclear diameter set as 20 pixels. The stitch mode was used with a stitch threshold of 0.4 to generate 3D nuclear segments. Nuclear segments were filtered by size (1000–5000 pixels) and height (>10 μm), while those located at the edge of the imaging area were excluded for data processing. The regionprops function implemented in the Skimage Python library was used to define the bounding box of each nuclear segment, from which the middle Z coordinate of the bounding box was designated as the nuclear position. For time alignment, t0 (the onset of gastrulation) was defined as the time point, at which apical constriction in ventral furrow produces a 2.5 μm gap between the cell apex and vitelline membrane for the datasets acquired on the ventral side. Using this t0 designation (from water-injected embryos imaged on the ventral side), the pre-injection cellularization depths were fitted to a linear function based on the assumption that cellularization depth is linear with time during mid-cellularization. For datasets acquired on the lateral and dorsal sides, the pre-injection timing relative to the onset of gastrulation was derived by plugging in the pre-injection cellularization depth, from which the t0 frame of the dataset was derived. Data processing and plotting were performed with custom-made Python codes using Numpy, Pandas, Matplotlib, and Seaborn libraries.

For en face membrane visualization, 3xmScarlet-CaaX images were deconvolved using the Huygens Software (Scientific Volume Imaging) with the deconvolution algorithm Classic MLE using custom parameter sets.

Thank you for submitting your article "Differential regulation of the proteome and phosphoproteome along the dorso-ventral axis of the early Drosophila embryo" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers at Review Commons, and the evaluation at eLife has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Claude Desplan as the Senior Editor.

Based on the previous reviews and the revisions, the manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below:

1. Although the manuscript is easier to read, it is still convoluted for a non-specialist audience, and further clarifications throughout the manuscript are needed.

2. Statistical considerations: statistics have been added as supplementary tables, however they are separated from the main figures, and they should instead be included together with the figures, at least in the legends. At the very least, a description of statistical analysis, what the number of asterisks means, etc. should be included in the figure legends.

3. The observed Toll and Cactus phosphorylation still make little biological sense in terms of the expected effects based on the specific genetic perturbations used. The biological insight based on these data is difficult to distill, despite the provided explanation in the rebuttal (perhaps some of it should be included in the paper). Moreover, why are these examples used as evidence for successful identification of relevant phosphosites?

4. The data presented in Fig. 6 are still confusing because no attempts are made to analyze or present the observed GO categories as functional groups (e.g. by highlighting or some other means). The text refers to some groups but it is difficult to extract this information from the current version of the figure.

5. The suggestion to include information and references for the genes and alleles used in this work early on in the text has not been addressed, but this is important because the choice of the alleles is foundational for the design of the study. Multiple genes and alleles are mentioned in the Introduction and Results on pages 3-4 without references or explaining how specific alleles disrupt gene function. Including this information in the Methods section is not sufficient, and it is critical to explain the rationale for using these specific alleles and combinations and refer to prior work. The authors mention Table 1 but such a table did not appear in the revised manuscript, and Supplemental Table 1 does not provide the relevant information.

6. Some Supplemental Tables (e.g. Supp. Table 7) contain many gene/protein identifiers labeled as "NaN" - it would be worth ensuring that there have been no errors in making these tables.

results.result: The study detected 6111 protein groups and 6259 phosphosites, with 3398 protein groups and 3433 phosphosites differentially regulated across five populations (wildtype and four mutants). The number of proteins detected in wildtype embryos (5883) exceeded previously reported numbers from early Drosophila embryogenesis. Most proteins were detected in all genotypes, while 519 proteins had restricted detection including known DV fate determinants. Statistical analysis showed 28% of proteins and 9% of phosphosites differed significantly across populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6, C117-C123 provide comprehensive quantitative measurements from the proteomic and phosphoproteomic experiments. The data are internally consistent, include appropriate statistical testing (ANOVA with permutation-based FDR), and are supported by figures showing detection across genotypes. The comparison to previous studies (C118) provides validation of the improved depth of coverage.

results.result: Changes in phosphosite abundance did not correlate with changes in host protein abundance, indicating phosphorylation acts as a regulatory step during gastrulation. Analysis showed 67-82% of protein-phosphosite pairs had phosphorylation changes without corresponding protein level changes, while only 7-13% changed in the same direction and 10-19% changed in opposite directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C136-C139 demonstrate through quantitative correlation analysis that phosphorylation regulation is largely independent of protein abundance changes. The percentages are clearly defined and the conclusion that phosphorylation is a regulatory mechanism is well-supported by the data shown in Figure 5B. This represents a key finding about post-translational regulation during gastrulation.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering of protein groups identified 14 clusters containing known fate determinants (Doc1, Sog, Snail, Twist). While six clusters were expected based on known DV expression patterns, eight additional clusters emerged due to differences between the two ventralizing mutants (Toll10B and spn27A). Most marker proteins were found in their predicted classes, validating the approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C189-C193 describe the clustering analysis and validation. The recovery of known markers in appropriate clusters (C10, C193) validates the experimental approach. The unexpected finding of 14 rather than 6 clusters (C189-C191) is well-documented and attributed to differences between ventralizing mutants, which is further explored in other results. The clustering methodology is clearly described and results are shown in Figure 3.

results.result: Toll10B and spn27A mutations, both causing ventralization, interfere with the dorsal fate pathway in different manners. While both recapitulated mesodermal biological qualities, their proteomes differed significantly. The spn27A proteome was more similar to dorsalized than to Toll10B, yet mesodermal markers (snail, twist, mdr49, wntD, neur) were more abundant in spn27A. Toll10B mutants failed to repress ectodermal genes (egr, zen, crb) as strongly as spn27A.
results.evaluation: Claims C11 and C97-C102, C132-C133 document an important biological finding about differential effects of two ventralizing mutations. The proteomic data clearly show quantitative differences between Toll10B and spn27A embryos despite similar morphological phenotypes. The correlation analysis (Figure 3E) and specific protein measurements support the conclusion that these mutations affect the pathway differently. This is a well-supported discovery with mechanistic implications.

results.result: Diffused network analyses identified microtubule components as one of the main groups of regulated proteins. Networks enriched for cytoskeletal components were much more prevalent in phosphoproteomes (14 of 62) than proteomes (3 of 63), with microtubules strongly represented (12 of 14 cellular components). Both experiments were highly enriched for cellular components associated with DNA/RNA metabolism and gene expression regulation, with the majority characterized as nuclear ontology classes.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C29, C151-C155 describe the network analysis results. The quantitative enrichment data (C154-C155) clearly show differential representation of cytoskeletal/microtubule components in phosphoproteomes versus proteomes. The ego network analysis methodology is described and yielded 83 ontology terms in proteome and 87 in phosphoproteome (C151). The enrichment for gene expression machinery (C152-C153) validates the approach for this developmental stage. Results are supported by Figure 6 and supplementary files.

results.result: Functional studies demonstrate that microtubules have different functions in different domains along the DV axis during gastrulation. MTs are required for correct nuclear positioning and cell shape homeostasis, with distinct functional requirements in all three types of epithelial folds. Colcemid treatment caused ventral furrow formation to fail, dorsal fold formation to fail, but only delayed cephalic furrow formation without affecting its progress.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C64-C65, C92, C94, C50, C57-C58 describe functional validation experiments using colcemid to depolymerize microtubules. The differential effects on ventral furrow (complete failure), cephalic furrow (delay but normal progression), and dorsal fold (failure) clearly demonstrate region-specific MT functions. Live imaging data (Figure 7, Videos 1-3) provide strong visual evidence. The conclusion that MTs have distinct functional requirements in different DV domains is well-supported by the perturbation experiments.

results.result: A linear model was developed based on the assumption that each mutant represents a defined DV region, predicting that weighted mutant protein abundances should sum to wildtype values. The model was validated: the majority of proteins had deviations around zero, and even ANOVA-significant proteins fell within ±0.5 deviation (less than 1.4-fold). The majority of phosphosites also fitted the linear model.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112, C185-C187, C140 describe the development and validation of the linear model. The analytical approach is clearly explained (C111), and the validation data show that most proteins fit the model well (C185-C187). The extension to phosphosites (C140) further validates the approach. The model provides a rigorous framework for interpreting the data and identifying proteins that deviate from expected patterns, which may indicate non-autonomous regulation. The methodology is sound and results are shown in Figures 3A and 5C.

results.result: Comparison of proteomic clusters with single-cell RNA sequencing data showed that the majority of proteins had perfect or partial matches with RNA expression patterns. For example, 9 of 13 proteins in ventral cluster 5 matched the 'twist' RNA reference group. Clusters where Toll10B and spn27A agreed showed larger proportions allocated to correct RNA reference sets than inconsistent clusters. Proteins with strong fold-changes were more likely to match correct RNA patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C208-C213, C224-C225 describe validation of proteomic clustering against independent RNA expression data. The quantitative matching data (C209-C210) and systematic comparison (C213) demonstrate good concordance between protein and RNA measurements. The finding that consistent ventralizing mutant clusters better match RNA patterns (C213, C224) and that larger fold-changes correlate with better RNA matching (C225) provide important quality metrics. The analysis is rigorous and results are shown in Figure 4.

results.result: Constitutively active Toll (Toll10B mutation) does not lead to the same level of signaling as ligand-receptor binding (spn27A mutation), resulting in unexpected differences in downstream targets. Although Toll10B mutants are strongly ventralized, ectopic Toll signaling fails to suppress all dorsal markers. spn27A mutants show stronger reduction in dorsal-specific proteins and retain no or almost no DV polarity, whereas Toll10B embryos retain residual polarity.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110, C217-C220 describe an important mechanistic finding about Toll pathway signaling. The proteomic differences between Toll10B and spn27A (C109-C110, C217-C218) are well-documented quantitatively. The interpretation that spn27A represents more complete loss of DV polarity while Toll10B retains residual polarity (C219-C220) is supported by both the current data and cited prior work. This provides new insight into how different mutations in the same pathway can have quantitatively different effects on downstream targets.

results.result: Before gastrulation, all cells have two MT subpopulations: a disordered apical network of non-centrosomal dynamic MTs (marked by tyrosinated α-tubulin) and an inverted basket of basal-lateral MTs from centrosomes (containing stable MTs marked by acetylated α-tubulin). During gastrulation, MT acetylation patterns change: ectodermal MTs become increasingly acetylated while retaining organization, whereas central mesodermal basal-lateral MTs become less acetylated.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 describe MT organization and dynamics during gastrulation. The characterization of two MT populations (C38-C40) is supported by both cited literature and imaging data in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A. The changes during gastrulation (C41-C43) are documented by imaging in Figure 7B. The combination of established knowledge with new observations about acetylation changes provides a clear picture of MT dynamics during this developmental transition.

results.result: Colcemid injection caused rapid MT depolymerization (within 1 min), with most apical filamentous structures and centrosomes disappearing while stable nuclear envelope-associated MTs were partially retained. This disrupted normal nuclear positioning during cellularization and affected morphogenetic processes differently across DV regions: nuclear positioning became more random in ventral furrow cells, cephalic furrow formation was delayed by 5 min but progressed normally, and the apical dome in dorsal cells was abolished, supporting that MT-dependent force is required for apical dome formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47, C49, C51-C52, C54-C55 describe the immediate and downstream effects of colcemid treatment. The rapid depolymerization (C44-C45) is documented by live imaging (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D). The differential effects on nuclear positioning (C46-C47, C49) and morphogenetic processes (C51-C52, C54) are quantified and shown in Figure 7 and Videos 1-3. The inference that MT-dependent force is required for apical dome formation (C55) is reasonable based on the abolishment of the dome upon MT depolymerization. The temporal resolution and quantitative measurements support these conclusions.

results.result: Many proteins show differences in abundance across DV populations that do not match RNA abundance differences, and region-specific phosphorylation patterns exist in ubiquitously expressed proteins. P-granule-related networks were enriched in both proteome and phosphoproteome, particularly in DV clusters with ectodermal fate that show strong mRNA-protein uncoupling. This uncoupling appears to be the rule rather than exception in ectodermal and neuroectodermal tissues (97.5% of studied genes in larval tissues), highlighting the importance of post-transcriptional regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28, C86-C89 describe post-transcriptional regulation mechanisms. The observation of protein-RNA discordance (C27) is supported by comparison with RNA data. The enrichment of P-granule networks in clusters showing mRNA-protein uncoupling (C86-C87) provides a mechanistic link. The citation of similar findings in larval tissues (C88) and the inference about the prevalence of post-transcriptional regulation (C89) are well-supported. The network analysis (Figure 6B) provides additional evidence. This represents an important finding about developmental gene regulation.

results.result: In situ hybridization validated that mutant embryos represent distinct DV cell populations: dorsalized and lateralized embryos expressed neither twist nor snail, while ventralized embryos expressed both around their entire circumference. In lateralized embryos, sog expanded dorsally and ventrally while dpp expanded ventrally. Proteomic analysis confirmed these patterns, with ventral markers (Snail, Twist, Mdr49, Traf4, CG4500) more abundant in ventralized embryos, lateral marker Sog in lateralized embryos, and dorsal markers (Zen, Doc1, Dtg, Net, Egr) in dorsalized embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35, C129-C131 provide validation that mutant embryos faithfully represent DV cell populations. The in situ hybridization data (C32-C35, Figure 1B) and proteomic measurements (C129-C131, Figure 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D) are concordant and demonstrate that known DV markers are appropriately enriched in corresponding mutants. This validation is essential for the entire study's premise that mutants can be used to represent DV regions. The data are clear and well-documented.

results.result: Cellular validation showed that mutant cells recapitulate wildtype DV cell behaviors: adherens junctions relocalized apically in ventralized mutants, remained apico-lateral in lateralized, and shifted basally in dorsalized mutants. The apical actomyosin network formed a pulsatile network in ventralized embryos, accumulated at junctions in lateralized embryos, and dissolved in dorsalized embryos. These observations demonstrate that mutant cell populations are good sources for analyzing proteomic and phosphoproteomic composition of natural cell populations at gastrulation onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C167 provide crucial validation of the experimental system through cell biological observations. The adherens junction localization (C160-C162, Figure 1C) and actomyosin organization (C163-C165, Figure 1E-F) in mutants mirror known behaviors in corresponding wildtype regions. The inference that mutants are appropriate for proteomic analysis (C166-C167) is well-justified by this validation. This establishes confidence in using mutants as proxies for DV regions, which is fundamental to the study design.

results.result: Analysis of the Rho signaling pathway detected 21 of 24 associated proteins in wildtype and mutants. Most proteins, including myosin light chain, occurred at similar levels across genotypes, except Cofilin/Twinstar, Moesin, and Profilin/chickadee, which were more abundant in ectodermal populations. Fourteen proteins were phosphorylated, including known phosphosites in MLC and Cofilin/Twinstar, with LIMK1, Slingshot, RhoGEF2, and Mbs phosphorylation modulated in dorsal and dorso-lateral clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C148 describe comprehensive analysis of a well-characterized pathway relevant to gastrulation. The detection of 21/24 Rho pathway proteins (C144) demonstrates good coverage. The differential abundance of specific proteins (C145) and phosphorylation patterns (C146-C148) are documented in Figure 5E-F. This provides both validation (detecting known phosphosites) and new information (differential phosphorylation of regulators) about Rho pathway regulation during gastrulation. The analysis is thorough and well-supported.

results.result: Comparison with a previous 2D gel electrophoresis study showed all 37 previously identified proteins were detected in the current proteomes. Of proteins with variable isoforms, 15 were phosphorylated in the current study, with 7 showing differences in mutants consistent with the 2D-PAGE experiment. Known phosphosites were detected in Rho pathway proteins (Sqh-T21, Sqh-S22, Cofilin-S3) and in proteins involved in gastrulation (LIMK1, RhoGEF2) and DV axis establishment (Toll-S871, Cactus-S463/467/468).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C76 provide validation through comparison with prior work and detection of known phosphosites. The complete recovery of previously identified proteins (C68) and consistency of phosphorylation patterns (C69-C70) validate the current methodology. Detection of known phosphosites (C71-C76) with appropriate spatial patterns (e.g., Toll-S871 more abundant in ventralized embryos, C75) demonstrates both technical success and biological relevance. The data are supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and cited literature.

results.result: Network analysis identified the cullin complex as differentially expressed and differentially regulated. Neur, an E3-ubiquitin ligase known to be required and upregulated in prospective mesoderm, was found in increased abundance ventrally.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 identify protein degradation machinery as differentially regulated along the DV axis. The detection of cullin complex differential regulation (C84, Figure 6A) and ventral enrichment of Neur (C85) are consistent with known biology of Neur in mesoderm. This validates the network analysis approach and identifies the ubiquitin-proteasome system as a mechanism for creating DV differences. While these are supporting findings for the broader network analysis, they represent biologically meaningful observations.

results.result: Strong deviations from the linear model may indicate non-autonomous regulation. Ind, a protein known to be regulated by input from neighboring regions, showed high deviation (2.6) with higher than predicted expression in dorsalized and ventralized mutants. TM9SF4, an immune-related transporter, showed extreme deviation with nearly 100-fold higher levels in all mutants versus wildtype. However, stress-related categories represented only a small percentage of proteins with highest deviations.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 explore deviations from the linear model. The speculation about non-autonomous regulation (C113) is reasonable and supported by the example of Ind (C114), which is known to require input from neighboring regions. The extreme case of TM9SF4 (C115) likely represents a stress response, but the analysis shows this is not a general pattern (C116, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E). The interpretation is appropriately cautious and the data support the conclusions about what deviations might indicate.

results.result: Quality control analysis showed that for the proteome, replicates from the same genotypes clustered together. For the phosphoproteome, the first replicate of each genotype separated from the other two replicates, but all replicates were retained because the experimental source of variation could not be determined.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C172 describe quality control and a methodological decision. The correlation analysis (Figure 2E-F) clearly shows the described patterns. The decision to retain all phosphoproteome replicates (C172) is reasonable given the inability to identify the source of variation and the need for adequate statistical power. This represents appropriate transparency about data quality and analytical decisions, though it does introduce some uncertainty into the phosphoproteome results.

results.result: Microtubule forces engage in cell shortening during dorsal fold formation, as supported by colcemid experiments and prior literature. Ventral furrow and dorsal fold formation differ in myosin dependency but both require microtubules for basal nuclear relocalization. This requirement is functionally distinct from MT-actomyosin association during myosin-dependent folding and may relate to MT roles in vectorial trafficking and organelle localization. One reason nuclei need repositioning may be that apical nuclei constitute a physical barrier to apical constriction.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C93, C95-C96 integrate experimental findings with prior knowledge and provide mechanistic interpretation. The role of MT forces in dorsal fold formation (C59) is supported by colcemid experiments and cited literature. The comparison of ventral furrow and dorsal fold requirements (C93) synthesizes current and prior findings. The interpretation about functional distinction from actomyosin association (C95) and speculation about nuclear positioning (C96) are reasonable based on the data and established MT functions. The reasoning is sound though some aspects remain speculative.

results.result: Colcemid treatment caused enlarged membrane blebs in apical membranes of constricting mesodermal cells and excessive tortuous subapical membrane accumulation in lateral and dorsal cells. A distinct class of micron-scale membrane blebs was observed in all dorsal cells during mid-to-late cellularization, which exclude MTs and are stable for minutes. These distinct phenotypes suggest differential functionality in membrane-cortex attachment or apical membrane retrieval dynamics for MT networks on different embryo sides.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63, C66 describe membrane phenotypes following MT depolymerization. The observations of enlarged blebs (C60), excessive membrane (C61), and dorsal-specific blebs (C62-C63) are documented in Figure 7N-O. The interpretation about differential MT network functionality (C66) is speculative but reasonable given the distinct regional phenotypes. These observations provide additional evidence for region-specific MT functions, though the mechanistic interpretation remains uncertain and would benefit from further investigation.

results.result: Background knowledge about Drosophila gastrulation: The initially homogeneous epithelium differentiates into regional subpopulations with different behaviors needed for morphogenesis. Top genetic hierarchy factors are known but many targets are not. Gastrulation initiates with ventral furrow formation leading to mesoderm internalization, causing ventral neuroectoderm displacement accommodated by dorsal cell stretching. Most cellular components pre-exist maternally, and phosphorylation plays key roles in early embryogenesis including Toll/Dpp pathway regulation and Rho pathway activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C14-C23 provide established background knowledge about Drosophila development, supported by cited literature. These claims set the context for the study and are well-established facts in the field. They accurately describe the developmental biology, the genetic hierarchy, and the role of phosphorylation in early embryogenesis. This background is essential for understanding the study's rationale and significance.

results.result: Prior studies of DV axis differences used transcriptomic and proteomic methods but with limited depth and temporal resolution. Studies of temporal changes identified proteins appearing during maternal-to-zygotic transition and later embryogenesis but lacked spatial specificity. None addressed region-specific post-translational regulation of proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 accurately characterize limitations of prior work, supported by cited references. These claims establish the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses: the lack of comprehensive, spatially-resolved proteomic and phosphoproteomic data during gastrulation. This justifies the study's approach and significance.

results.result: The gd9 allele generates the strongest dorsalization without affecting embryo length. Mothers transheterozygous for Tlrm9 and Tlrm10 produce lateralized embryos where the entire DV axis forms neuroectoderm.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 describe the genetic tools used, supported by cited literature. These are established properties of these mutant alleles and provide justification for their selection in the experimental design. The information is accurate and appropriately referenced.

results.result: Ventralized embryos showed some variation in gene expression patterns: they often had a gap in snail expression in a small dorsal-anterior domain around the procephalic furrow where sog expression was detected instead, suggesting retention of some neuroectodermal fate cells in a restricted area.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 describe observed variation in ventralized embryos. The detection of sog expression in the region lacking snail (C37) provides evidence for the inference about retained neuroectodermal fate. This observation is important for interpreting the proteomic data and acknowledging that the ventralization is not completely uniform. The inference is reasonable based on the marker gene expression.

results.result: Established knowledge about microtubules in Drosophila morphogenesis: Dorsal epithelium forms folds depending on apical MT remodeling but not myosin contractility. In epithelial tissues, microtubules are often required for cell shape homeostasis. Morphogenetic cell shape changes requiring microtubules include amnioserosa squamous morphogenesis, mesoderm invagination, and salivary placode invagination.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C90-C91 provide established background about MT functions in Drosophila, supported by cited literature. This background contextualizes the current study's findings about MT roles in gastrulation and validates the focus on microtubules identified through network analysis. The information is accurate and appropriately referenced.

results.result: Comparison with prior RNA expression studies shows mixed concordance: An Affymetrix study identified 23 ventrally upregulated genes, but comparison with single-cell RNA-seq reveals 5 have little DV modulation. Genes identified by genetic/functional studies show up in all studies. The current study detected proteins for 13 of 17 genes seen as ventrally upregulated in both prior studies, with all but 4 seen as ventrally upregulated. Traf4, active in mesoderm but expressed at low levels, was strongly downregulated in dorsalized embryos but showed only sub-threshold upregulation in ventralized embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 provide careful comparison with prior RNA expression studies, acknowledging discrepancies between different methods (C77-C78) while showing general concordance for well-studied genes (C79-C81). The example of Traf4 (C82-C83) illustrates challenges in comparing protein and RNA data and the importance of considering expression levels. This analysis appropriately acknowledges limitations in RNA-protein comparisons while demonstrating overall consistency for major markers.

results.result: Mechanistic background on Toll pathway mutations: Spn27A is a serine protease inhibitor in the pathway creating active Spätzle (Spz), Toll's ligand. Both Toll10B and spn27A mutations lead to constitutive Toll activity, but through different mechanisms: Toll10B through receptor mutation, spn27A through enabling homogeneously high Spz levels. Since Spz is highly abundant and not limiting, loss of Spn27A should enable full Toll activation along the DV axis.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C108 provide mechanistic background about the Toll pathway mutations, supported by cited literature and proteomic data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). This background is essential for interpreting the differential effects of Toll10B versus spn27A mutations. The reasoning about Spz abundance and expected Toll activation (C107-C108) is sound and sets up the surprising finding that the two mutations have different downstream effects.

results.result: Quantitative characterization of protein changes: Enrichment for proteins or phosphosites in mutants versus wildtype ranged from near-zero to 100-fold, with about half changing less than 1.5-fold. The largest positive fold-changes among DV fate determinants were Snail (7.7-fold) and Twist (14.6-fold) in spn27Aex/def embryos. Both Toll and Spn27A proteins were detected and reduced in abundance in respective mutant embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C128 provide quantitative characterization of the dynamic range and specific examples of protein changes. The fold-change distributions (C124-C125, Figure 2G-H) establish the scale of changes observed. The specific values for Snail and Twist (C126-C127) provide benchmarks for major DV determinants. Detection of reduced Toll and Spn27A in respective mutants (C128) validates the genetic manipulations. These quantitative details support the overall findings.

results.result: Overlap between proteome and phosphoproteome: 1765 phosphoproteins (96%) were also found in the proteome, while 82 had not been detected in the proteome.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 describe the overlap between proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets, shown in Figure 5A. The high overlap (96%) indicates good concordance between the two experiments, while the 82 phosphoproteins not detected in the proteome may represent low-abundance proteins enriched through phosphopeptide enrichment. This characterization is straightforward and well-supported.

results.result: Phosphoproteome analysis revealed strongly deviating phosphoproteins including kinases with known morphogenetic functions (Par-1, SRC42A, nucleoside-diphosphate kinase/awd). In phosphoproteome clustering, the two ventralizing mutants clustered together and the dorsalized mutant showed the most distinct behavior, contrasting with the proteome where ventralizing mutants were more separated.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C143 describe phosphoproteome-specific findings. The identification of morphogenetically relevant kinases among deviating phosphoproteins (C141) is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E. The different clustering pattern in phosphoproteome versus proteome (C142-C143, Figure 5G vs 3E) is an interesting observation suggesting that phosphorylation patterns may be more consistent between ventralizing mutants than total protein levels. This supports the idea that phosphorylation provides an additional regulatory layer.

results.result: Network analysis methodology and specific findings: A diffusion-based algorithm was applied to DV clusters, with protein weights based on Euclidean distance scores or deviation from linear model. The cell cortex was among enriched components, with cytoskeletal elements found in this category. Specific networks were enriched in particular clusters: Shot and Profilin in dorsal cluster; Stardust and Warts in dorso-lateral cluster; adherens junction-associated phosphoproteins including Canoe and Girdin in dorsal cluster.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C150, C156-C159 describe network analysis methods and specific findings. The methodology (C149-C150) is clearly explained. The enrichment of cell cortex components (C156) and specific examples of networks in particular clusters (C157-C159) demonstrate that the analysis identifies biologically meaningful protein associations relevant to known cellular structures and processes. These findings are supported by the data in Figure 6 and Supplementary file 12.

results.result: Experimental procedures: Embryos were synchronized and manually collected from wildtype and mutant mothers aged 165-180 minutes at 25°C (Stage 6). Peptides and phospho-peptides were analyzed with label-free quantification (LFQ) and SILAC. The proteomic and phosphoproteomic screen correctly identified known and differentially expressed proteins and phosphosites.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C169, C173 describe key experimental procedures and validation. The careful staging and manual selection (C168) ensures developmental synchrony. The use of both LFQ and SILAC (C169) provides robust quantification. The summary statement about correct identification of known markers (C173) is supported by the validation data throughout the results. These methodological details are essential for reproducibility.

results.result: Linear model explanation using Snail as example: The assumption that each mutant represents a defined embryo region predicts that summed weighted mutant protein quantities should equal wildtype amounts. Snail exemplifies ideal behavior: expressed only in prospective mesoderm (ventral domain) in wildtype, practically in all cells of ventralized embryos, and nowhere in lateralized and dorsalized embryos. This pattern is correctly reflected in the proteomes, with Snail absent in dorsalized and lateralized proteomes and higher in ventralized embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C180 use Snail as a clear example to explain the linear model concept. The spatial expression pattern (C175-C177, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and proteomic measurements (C178-C179, Figure 1D) demonstrate perfect concordance. This example effectively illustrates why the linear model should work for proteins with region-specific expression and validates the approach. The reasoning is clear and well-supported.

results.result: Linear model parameter optimization: Optimal proportions for dorsal and lateral populations were determined analytically. For Snail, the deviation value is 1.07 when Toll10B represents 'ventral', but 2.91 when spn27A represents 'ventral', indicating spn27A may over-represent the ventral population.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C184 describe the analytical determination of model parameters and application to Snail. The optimization approach (C181) is explained in Methods. The specific deviation values for Snail (C182-C183) and interpretation about spn27A (C184) are consistent with other findings that spn27A produces more complete ventralization. This analysis provides quantitative support for the qualitative observation that the two ventralizing mutants differ in their effects.

results.result: Proteins with the most extreme deviations (more than twofold) from the linear model did not come from any well-defined class but represented a wide range of ontologies.
results.evaluation: Claim C188 describes the ontology analysis of extremely deviating proteins, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 13. The finding that extreme deviations are not confined to specific protein classes suggests diverse mechanisms can cause deviations from the linear model, rather than a single systematic issue. This observation is straightforward and well-documented.

results.result: Analysis of proteins in clusters where ventralizing mutants differed: Among proteins allocated to these clusters, there was no general rule as to which mutant represented the correct value. For example, Heartless and Net are both expressed in mesoderm and dorsal side, but Heartless showed increased abundance only in serpin27A embryos while Net only in Toll10B embryos. Similarly, for genes excluded from mesoderm, some were reduced in serpin27A (e.g., crb) while others in Toll10B (e.g., numb).
results.evaluation: Claims C194-C199 describe the complexity of interpreting clusters where ventralizing mutants disagree. The specific examples of Heartless and Net (C195-C198) and crb and numb (C199) illustrate that the differences between Toll10B and spn27A are not systematic but protein-specific. This observation is supported by the data in Figure 3D and highlights the biological complexity revealed by comparing the two ventralizing mutations.

results.result: Comparison with BDGP in situ database: Regional protein distribution in early Drosophila embryo is thought to be achieved mainly through transcriptional regulation. Of 109 genes with ventral expression labels in BDGP, 107 had proteins detected and 71 were allocated to DV clusters. Sixty were in clusters fully or partially consistent with reported RNA patterns. Of 11 proteins in DV cluster 5 showing consistent mesodermal upregulation in both ventralizing mutants, all are reported as ventrally expressed in BDGP.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C204 describe validation against the BDGP database. The high detection rate (107/109, C201) and good concordance (60/71 in consistent clusters, C203) demonstrate that the proteomic data generally match known RNA expression patterns. The perfect concordance for cluster 5 (C204) validates the clustering for the most clearly ventral proteins. This comparison provides important validation while acknowledging the expected role of transcriptional regulation (C200).

results.result: Analysis of single-cell RNA atlas: Filtering out ubiquitously expressed genes left 8924 differentially expressed genes, of which 3086 coded for 3120 proteins in the clustered proteome dataset. Further filtering for clear DV differences yielded 155 genes forming six DV RNA reference sets.
results.evaluation: Claims C205-C207 describe the processing of single-cell RNA data for comparison with proteomics. The filtering steps (C205, C207) are clearly explained and shown in Figure 4B-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D. The overlap of 3086 genes between RNA atlas and proteome (C206) provides a substantial dataset for comparison. The methodology for creating RNA reference sets is sound and enables systematic comparison.

results.result: Pattern in ventral inconsistent clusters: Proteins classified based on upregulation in Toll10B (clusters 3,7,10,13) are often mismatched to genes with ectodermal expression (dorsal and/or lateral RNA), whereas this does not occur for proteins classified based on upregulation in spn27A (clusters 4,8,11,14).
results.evaluation: Claims C215-C216 identify a systematic pattern in how Toll10B and spn27A differ, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E. The finding that Toll10B-upregulated proteins often mismatch to ectodermal RNA while spn27A-upregulated proteins do not (C215-C216) provides additional evidence that Toll10B retains more ectodermal character than spn27A. This systematic analysis strengthens the conclusion about differential effects of the two mutations.

results.result: Euclidean distance analysis: Proteins with the lowest ED scores are closest to the most extreme protein in each cluster. Proteins from 'matching' groups had ED scores skewed towards lower values, indicating proteins with more extreme expression differences (low ED scores) are more likely to match the correct RNA expression pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C221-C223 describe the ED score analysis and its relationship to RNA-protein matching. The methodology (C221) is clearly explained. The finding that matching proteins have lower ED scores (C222-C223, Figure 4F) makes biological sense: proteins with larger fold-changes are more likely to be truly differentially expressed rather than representing noise. This analysis provides a useful metric for assessing confidence in protein assignments.
